cycleResult.label: Cycle result

cycleResult.stillOpen: no result yet, the cycle has not closed

otherSpending.label: Spending outside the cards
otherSpending.note: Cash and transfers from available money

openCycle.note_one: Closes on {{date}}, {{count}} day to go. The totals below are a floor: charges are still arriving and the interest has not been billed.
openCycle.note_other: Closes on {{date}}, {{count}} days to go. The totals below are a floor: charges are still arriving and the interest has not been billed.

errors.missingCategoryOrAccount: Choose a category and account before saving.
errors.saveFailed: The transaction could not be saved.
errors.invalidAmount: Enter a valid amount with up to two decimals.

categorize.title: Categorise this transaction
categorize.hint: This categorises only this transaction and is recorded as a manual decision: no merchant rule overwrites it later. Use the categorisation queue when everything from the merchant belongs to the same category.

review.title: Review queue
review.empty: No unresolved source records for this statement period.

queue.title: Categorisation queue
queue.failed: The rule could not be saved.
queue.hint: Choosing a category creates a rule: it applies to every transaction from that merchant, across all cycles, and reapplies itself on each import.
queue.expandHint: Open a row to see the charges as the statement printed them. The normalised key is no help in recognising anything; the dates, amounts and full description are.

patterns.title: Recurring spending
patterns.installmentsNote: Already counted in the instalment calendar
patterns.empty: Not enough cycles yet to detect recurrence.
patterns.hint: Recurring and stable are different things: a power bill returns every cycle but varies, which makes it unavoidable with room to move. Classifying needs at least 3 cycles.
patterns.occasionalNote: Occasional spending is spread across the {{count}} cycles on record, so the three figures can be compared: a merchant that appeared once does not cost that every month.
patterns.medianNote: The median is used rather than the average on purpose: one odd month must not move what gets charged every month.

baseline.title: Baseline per cycle
baseline.hint: Commitments only, never an average of past spending: averaging cycles that overspent just predicts overspending.
baseline.financingNote: Financing is derived from the balance still outstanding rather than carried from the previous cycle.
baseline.rateNote: Effective monthly rate applied: {{rate}}%, the rate the statement declares plus the taxes that ride on it, measured against what was actually charged.

installments.title: Instalment calendar
installments.meta: What lands without buying anything else
installments.openEndedNote: The last row is a monthly amount from that month onward rather than a single month: the statement publishes it that way because the plan outlasts its table.
installments.hint: Taken from the forward-instalment table each statement publishes, not from a projection of our own. It is already bought: the only thing that reduces it is time.

payoff.title: Payoff projection
payoff.neverClears: Paying the minimum never clears the debt
payoff.neverClearsBody: The minimum of {{minimum}} does not cover the interest, so the balance grows every cycle. Over {{cycles}} cycles it would go from {{from}} to {{to}}, with {{interest}} of interest accrued.
payoff.hint: Interest runs on the part of the previous balance left unpaid, not on this cycle's purchases: a purchase accrues nothing until its own statement falls due.
payoff.assumption: Assumes {{income}} of income and {{recurring}} of detected recurring spending per cycle, plus instalments already committed and any declared commitments. The Declared and Replaces columns show which part of the charges comes from a commitment and how much detected spending it takes the place of.

levers.title: Levers
levers.meta: What shortens the payoff, and by how much
levers.hint: Each row is measured by re-running the whole projection without that cost, not by dividing the balance: interest compounds, so removing something early is worth more than its face value.
levers.onlyRecurring: Only active recurring costs appear. An instalment cannot be cut because the purchase already happened, and one-off spending is already assumed to be zero.
levers.finding_one: The one that moves it most: stopping {{cost}}, {{amount}} per cycle. You are clear {{count}} cycle sooner and save {{interest}} of interest.
levers.finding_other: The one that moves it most: stopping {{cost}}, {{amount}} per cycle. You are clear {{count}} cycles sooner and save {{interest}} of interest.
levers.findingNone: No single recurring cost brings the finish line forward: with all of them it is {{baseline}} cycles. What moves it is the variable spending, not these.

notes.title: Plan notes
notes.failed: The note could not be saved.
notes.hint: These notes move no number. They exist so the reasoning does not live only in someone's memory: who each counterparty is, what the envelope is for, why one payment settles the previous statement.

commitments.title: Declared commitments
commitments.hint: A commitment is a cost you state because the detector cannot see it yet: a charge has to come back for three cycles before it counts as recurring. Each one says how it meets what has already been detected, so the same money is never counted twice.
commitments.failed: The commitment could not be saved.

effectHint.addition: A cost the detector will never see, because it is paid in cash or off the card entirely. Nothing is removed.
effectHint.override: Names a merchant: adds the declared amount and removes what was detected for that merchant. This is the right choice for something already charged to the card but too new for the detector to recognise, and the figure will not double once it does.
effectHint.substitution: Names categories: adds the declared amount and removes the detected recurring spending it takes the place of. This is the cash envelope case.
effectHint.termination: Says a cost stops: it charges nothing and removes that merchant's detected amount from the cycle you pick onward. The detector cannot work this out on its own - a plan with a counted number of instalments looks exactly like an endless one until the cycle it fails to appear in, and by then the projection has charged months too many.

resolved.title: Effect on cycle {{period}}
resolved.note: When what it replaces exceeds what it charges the net is negative, and the plan is a cut rather than another cost.

form.title: Declare a commitment
form.label: Name
form.feeHint: It is inside the amount the card charges and never appears as its own line.
form.categoriesHint: Choosing a parent category includes all of its children.
form.merchantHint: You pick a cost, not a merchant: the same person can receive two different things, and one says nothing about the other.
form.periodInvalid: A cycle is written year-month, for example 2026-09.

scorecard.title: Plan against reality
scorecard.hint: The projected payoff charges the commitments and assumes variable spending stops. That is a freeze scenario, not a forecast. This table shows how much of each cycle was spending the plan does not account for, and below are both endings: if it stops, and if it carries on.
scorecard.ifItCarriesOn: If it carries on at {{amount}} per cycle
scorecard.drift: The gap between those two endings costs {{amount}} of interest. That is what the discipline is worth, in money.
scorecard.spread: Variable spending ran from {{best}} in the best cycle to {{worst}} in the worst, averaging {{average}}.

food.title: What food costs
food.hint: Kept apart from the rest because it is the one large block still open to a decision. The amounts on the left are what the card was charged; the value is what was left for the food once the gateway fee is taken out.
food.spread: From the best cycle ({{best}}) to the worst ({{worst}}): the worst is {{percent}}% of the best.
food.share: The median is {{percent}}% of recurring income.
food.commission: Of everything spent on food, at least {{amount}} went to the gateway rather than the shop.
food.floorNote: “At least” is meant literally: the fee is only detectable when the transfer was for a round amount, so the real figure is that or higher.
food.targetCeiling: The envelope sits {{amount}} above what a normal cycle costs, so it is not a cut but a ceiling. It catches the bad cycles, like the one at {{worst}}. In force from {{from}}.
food.targetCut: The envelope sits {{amount}} below what a normal cycle costs, so it is a real cut and it will pinch. In force from {{from}}.

fx.title: Spending in dollars
fx.hint: Every other panel filters to pesos, which is right for adding up and leaves this spending out of every figure on the dashboard. Converting it needs a rate that was stated, for a day it was stated for: there are several simultaneous rates here, so a conversion without a date is not an approximation but an invented number that looks exactly like a real one on screen. A cycle with no rate declared before it says so rather than showing a total.
fx.currentRate: Latest declared: {{amount}} per dollar, as of {{date}}
fx.total: USD {{foreign}} in total. Of that, what falls in cycles with a declared rate is {{converted}}.
fx.typical: Median of the cycles that could be converted: {{amount}}.
fx.unconverted_one: {{count}} cycle went unconverted because no rate was declared before it.
fx.unconverted_other: {{count}} cycles went unconverted because no rate was declared before them.
fx.failed: The rate could not be saved.

anomalies.title: Cycles out of line
anomalies.empty: No recurring cost is out of line.
anomalies.hint: The projection charges the median of each recurring cost, and the median is right precisely because one odd month cannot move it. The catch is that nobody then sees the odd month. This shows it, and separates the three reasons a cycle can come in high, because they mean different things.

kindHint.catch-up: The previous cycle has no charge at all and this one came in near double: both were settled together. It is not a price rise, and the median absorbs it correctly.
kindHint.step-up: It rose and stayed up. The median is lagging, so the projection is charging too little. Worth declaring as a commitment that replaces the merchant.
kindHint.step-down: It fell and stayed down, confirmed by a later complete cycle. The median is running high.
kindHint.spike: A high cycle that came back down on its own, with nothing missing before it. The median is right and nothing needs doing.

anomalies.understated: The projection charges {{amount}} too little per cycle
anomalies.nothingToDo: Nothing to do: no recurring cost rose and stayed risen, so the projection is not charging too little on any of them.
anomalies.actionNeeded: At least one cost rose and held. The projection is charging too little: worth declaring it as a commitment that replaces that cost.

verdict.title: Where you are and where this is going
verdict.ifStops: If you stop the spending that is not fixed
verdict.ifCarriesOn: If it carries on as it has, {{amount}} per cycle
verdict.caveat: The date on the left is not a forecast: it is what happens if the spending that is not fixed stops entirely. The one on the right is what has actually been happening. The gap between them is the only thing you can change, and everything below explains where both numbers come from.

glossary.cycle: A cycle is a card statement period, not a calendar month. It closes late in the month and is paid in the first days of the next, so a purchase on the 28th can land on the following statement.
glossary.opening: How much debt the cycle starts with. It is exactly what was left unpaid from the cycle before: which is why, if you do not pay it all, one cycle's close becomes the next one's open and interest is charged on that.
glossary.closing: How much debt the cycle ends with, new charges and interest included. This figure is the next cycle's opening balance.
glossary.newCharges: Everything charged to the card in the cycle: spending that repeats, instalments of older purchases, and the commitments you declared.
glossary.financingCost: The interest the card charges on the part of the debt that went unpaid. It is not charged on the cycle's new purchases: a purchase is interest-free until its own statement falls due.
glossary.available: What is left of the income after everything already committed is paid. If it is negative, the fixed costs eat the salary before any decision is made.
glossary.effectiveRate: What it costs per month to owe money on the card, taxes included. The rate printed on the statement is lower because it excludes VAT on the interest and stamp duty: the effective one is what is actually paid.
glossary.median: The middle value, not the average. Used on purpose: one odd month must not move what is expected every month. An average would move.
glossary.recurring: A cost that comes back every cycle. It has to appear in at least three to count as recurring, because with two it cannot be told from coincidence.
glossary.variableSpending: Everything that is neither fixed nor an instalment: one-off purchases and costs that appear some months and not others. It is the part that can be decided.
glossary.installment: An instalment of something already bought. It cannot be cut: the purchase has happened and the statement will charge it until the plan ends.
glossary.floor: The floor is what a cycle costs before any decision: the sum of everything that comes back on its own. It is the figure income has to be compared against.
glossary.declared: A cost you stated because the detector cannot see it yet. A charge has to come back for three cycles before it counts as recurring.
glossary.displaced: Spending that was already detected and that this commitment replaces rather than adds to. Without it, declaring a cash envelope would look like new spending when it actually changes how existing spending is paid.
glossary.gatewayFee: The fee the payment gateway charges when you transfer to an alias with the card. It arrives inside the charge, never as its own line, so it has to be deduced. It is a percentage: consolidating payments does not reduce it.
glossary.stability: How even the amount is from month to month. Stable is nearly the same figure every time, variable moves, erratic swings. A subscription and an electricity bill both come back monthly, but only one is predictable.
glossary.statementDebt: What the cards say you owe at the close of their latest statement. Not the same as what was spent in the cycle: it is the accumulated balance.
glossary.openCycle: The cycle has not closed, so charges are still missing. The totals it shows are a floor, not the final figure.
glossary.catchUp: A month that went unpaid and was billed together with the next. It arrives as roughly double and looks like a price rise, but it is not.
glossary.freezeScenario: A scenario where spending that is not fixed stops entirely. Useful for knowing what it would take, not for forecasting what will happen.

decisions.sectionLabel: What you decided about the data
decisions.title: Decisions you can undo
decisions.hint: Every line here changed how the numbers read. They are together and reversible because several were inferred from a truncated name rather than from a fact: if one is wrong, it should be fixable without touching the database.
decisions.rulesNote: A rule says everything from that merchant belongs to that category, across all cycles, and reapplies itself on each import. Deleting it leaves those charges uncategorised.
decisions.aliasesNote: Two spellings you confirmed are one merchant. Undoing it splits the charges apart again and leaves them uncategorised, so the question returns to the queue.
decisions.manualNote: Categories set one charge at a time. No rule overwrites them, so a mistake here is permanent until you undo it.
decisions.confirmRule: Delete this rule? The charges from that merchant become uncategorised.
decisions.confirmAlias: Split these merchants? The charges divide and become uncategorised.
decisions.confirmManual: Undo this category? It goes back to whatever the merchant rule says, or to uncategorised.

demo.title: Demo with invented data
demo.body: No figure on this page is real: they come from a generated example that ships with the repository. It is read only, so anything that would save will refuse. To use it with your own data, clone it and run it on your machine, where your data stays.
